catalog_quote: [p.41] one spoken by the Kuikuro and the younger Matipu generations, and the other spoken by the Kalapalo and the Nahukwá. [p.44] The perception of culminative stress was considered in the domain of argument and head merging. [p.48] For Kalapalo, in a relation of argument and head merge, we have an F0 curve which starts out high and decreases in a constant manner until the end of the merge, regardless of the number of syllables of the resulting phonological word. [p.49] In argument and head merge (alligator#see), when the syllable is perceived as prominent, it is the initial syllable of this merge; F0 suffices to determine its perception. [p.50] This tells us that in the second pattern, when the initial syllable is not perceived as the most prominent, the non-initial syllable in which is perceived the prominence will present the duration parameter as its distinctive acoustic correlate . As such, we may say that duration is in a kind of ‘complementary distribution’ with regards to F0 in a rule that goes: perceive F0 as prominent in the beginning of merge; perceive duration as prominent in all other positions. ... Therefore, in Kuikuro, perception-wise, the point of interest is the boundary between argument and head; in Kalapalo, the point of interest lies in the boundary between [argument#head] merges.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Kalapalo-Nahukwa variety (the one spoken by the Nahukwa and, per DoBeS/ISA, present-day Matipu), prominence is described only within the [argument#head] merge (phonological word/phrase): F0 is high at the left edge and falls through the merge; the syllable perceived as prominent is the merge-initial syllable (cued by F0), otherwise a non-initial syllable cued by extra duration. This contrasts with the Kuikuro variety, where the prominent syllable is the last syllable of the argument before the head with the F0 peak on the next syllable (word-level: iambs L-to-R with final trochaic reversal, Becker et al. 2025). No citation-form word-stress rule is stated for the Kalapalo-Nahukwa variety; Becker et al. 2025 explicitly call its foot type 'unknown', possibly iambic with left-aligned tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Kalapalo 'Pattern 2': when the merge-initial syllable is not the prominent one, the prominent (non-initial) syllable is marked by greater duration (one case attributed to vowel coalescence across the word boundary, kanga+alamakilü). Study based on one male speaker per variety, 16 elicited sentences each.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is explicitly 'argument and head merging' (internal argument + verb, or noun + ergative postposition), i.e. phrase-level phonological words in connected sentences, not isolated citation forms. Basso 2008:251 adds for Kalapalo only that 'Stressed vowels are nasalized'.
new_statements.identity_note: ISO mzo / Glottolog mati1253 'Matipuhy' bundles the Matipu and Nahukwa groups, but linguistically Upper Xingu Carib has two varieties that cut across the ISO split: (a) Kuikuro + Uagihutu ('old Matipu'), and (b) Kalapalo + Nahukwa + present-day Matipu (DoBeS Kuikuro page; ISA 'Nahukwa': 'compartilham o mesmo dialeto com os Kalapalo e os Matipu'; Silva & Franchetto 2011:41 instead say younger Matipu speak the Kuikuro variety). The quoted stress description is of the 'Kalapalo' variety (speaker from a Kalapalo village), which by ISO falls under kuik1246 'Kuikuro-Kalapalo' but is the variety the Nahukwa (and most Matipu) speak; Nahukua 2014 accordingly calls the language 'Nafukua-Kalapalo' vs 'Matipu-Kuikuro'. No description based on Nahukwa or Matipu speakers' phonology exists to my knowledge. The Kuikuro variety (kuik1246) has a full word-stress analysis in Becker et al. 2025 (held).

sources.note: Two varieties: Kuikuro (+ Matipu) vs Kalapalo + Nahukwa, distinguished 'above all' by rhythm/prosody. Acoustic study of culminative stress in the domain of [argument#head] merges, one speaker per variety. Kuikuro: prominent syllable = last syllable of the internal argument before the verb, F0 peak on the following syllable (['σ # σ]). Kalapalo: F0 starts high and falls across the whole merge; prominent syllable is the INITIAL syllable of the merge (F0), or else a non-initial syllable marked by longer duration (F0 and duration in complementary distribution). sources.citation: Becker, Michael, Bruna Franchetto, Arawa Didi Kuikuro, Yanapa Mehinaku Kuikuro & Andrija Petrovic. 2025. The incoherent stress of Kuikuro. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 43: 2363-2393.
sources.note: Kuikuro variety only: iambs left-to-right with final trochaic reversal (default penult), tone displaced rightward. On the Kalapalo variety (= the one Nahukwa/Matipu speak): 'The foot type of Kalapalo is unknown, but an examination of a Swadesh list (Franchetto 2014) suggests that it is iambic' and 'Kalapalo might have iambic footing as in Kuikuro, but with tone that tends to align to left edges' (conclusion), citing da Silva & Franchetto 2011.

sources.citation: DoBeS Kuikuro documentation project (Franchetto et al.), 'Language' web page, dobes.mpi.nl/projects/kuikuro/language/
sources.note: 'The Upper Xingu Carib language has two main dialects: the one spoken by the Kuikuro and Uagihutu (old Matipu) people, and that spoken by the Kalapalo, Nahukwa and Matipu. These varieties can be distinguished by differences in lexicon and, above all, by differences in their rhythmic structures or prosody.' No stress position.

Observe-se a sensibilidade metalingüística às diferenças prosódicas entre as variantes karib alto-xinguanas. [...] Romling, Franchetto e Colamarco (2010) realizaram um estudo em fonética experimental que procura ‘traduzir’ as diferenças dialetais karib alto-xinguanas, rotuladas e comentadas pelos seus falantes, nos parâmetros acústicos e perceptivos relevantes, descobrindo uma distinção rítmica ‘dramática’ que resulta de padrões de distintas interpretações fonológicas de constituintes de uma mesma sintaxe frasal: enquanto a variante Kalapalo/Nahukwa/Matipu ‘lê’ fonologicamente as fronteiras entre sintagmas (constituintes compostos por um núcleo e seu argumento), a variante Kuikuro/Uagihütü interpreta fonologicamente os pontos de concatenação entre núcleos e seus argumentos. tone.locator: (sec. on dialect variants and prosody) (phonological sketch); document has no page numbers
tone.translation: [p.14] the Carib dialect spoken by the Kalapalo and the Nahukwá is described as being spoken 'in curves' (tühenkgegiho) or 'at the bottom' (inhukilüi) (Franchetto 1986). Note the metalinguistic sensitivity to the prosodic differences between the Upper Xingu Carib variants. [...] Romling, Franchetto and Colamarco (2010) carried out an experimental-phonetic study that seeks to 'translate' the Upper Xingu Carib dialect differences, labelled and commented on by their speakers, into the relevant acoustic and perceptual parameters, finding a 'dramatic' rhythmic distinction that results from patterns of distinct phonological interpretations of constituents of one and the same phrasal syntax: whereas the Kalapalo/Nahukwa/Matipu variant phonologically 'reads' the boundaries between phrases (constituents made of a head and its argument), the Kuikuro/Uagihütü variant phonologically interprets the points of concatenation between heads and their arguments. tone.summary: No lexical tone; phrase-level prosody in which F0 is the primary cue of rhythmic patterning aligned to phrase boundaries (Kalapalo/Nahukwa/Matipu variant).
